original_question: Let fT : PN → PN be a family of dominant rational maps, depending rationally on a list of parameters T = (T1 , . . . , Tk ). Then for all ǫ > 0, the set (14.2) t ∈ Ck : δ(ft ) ≤ δ(f ) − ǫ is not Zariski dense in Ck . In particular, for one-parameter families, i.e., k = 1, the set (14.2) is finite. One approach to proving Conjecture 14.13 would be to prove the following uniform lower bound for δf , from which it is easy to deduce Conjecture 14.13; see [47, 236].
target_in_paper: Conjecture 14.13 in Section 14 (Dynamical Degrees of Rational Maps), with nearby context from Definition 14.2 and Example 14.12; the draft also alludes to, but does not actually state, the adjacent sufficient criterion Conjecture 14.14.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly targets the family-variation conjecture for dynamical degrees of dominant rational self-maps of P^N. It accurately includes the exceptional set {t in C^k : delta(f_t) <= delta(f) - epsilon}, the claim that this set should not be Zariski dense, and the special one-parameter consequence that the exceptional set should be finite. It also correctly notices the neighboring discussion that Conjecture 14.14 would imply Conjecture 14.13.
missing_details: The draft does not identify the official target by label: it is Conjecture 14.13, not Conjecture 14.14.
The notation delta(g) is not defined. In Section 14, delta(g) is the dynamical degree delta(g) = lim_{n->infinity} deg(g^n)^(1/n) for a dominant rational map g of P^N.

The unsubscripted f in delta(f) is left implicit. In the paper's family notation, this is naturally read as the generic member of the family, i.e. the map over the function field C(T_1,...,T_k), while f_t denotes the specialization at t.
To be stand-alone, the family should be described as a rational family over C: the homogeneous coordinate functions depend rationally on T = (T_1,...,T_k).

The projective-space setup is implicit. Section 14 works specifically with dominant rational self-maps of P^N; this should not be broadened to arbitrary varieties, since the generalization to smooth projective varieties appears only later in Section 14.1.

The meaning of deg(g) for a rational map of P^N is omitted. In the nearby context, a rational map is given by homogeneous coordinate forms of the same degree, with common factors removed, and that common degree is deg(g).

The draft does not say explicitly that the specialization f_t must be defined and dominant for delta(f_t) to make sense; this is a hidden assumption that should be made explicit in a stand-alone formulation.

The final sentence mixes the official conjecture with a neighboring sufficient approach. In the paper, Conjecture 14.14 is presented only as one route to proving Conjecture 14.13, not as an equivalent reformulation.
refined_question: Let f_T = [F_0(T;X_0,...,X_N):...:F_N(T;X_0,...,X_N)] be a family of dominant rational self-maps of P^N over C, where the F_i are homogeneous of the same degree in X_0,...,X_N and their coefficients are rational functions of the parameters T = (T_1,...,T_k). Let f denote the induced dominant rational map over the function field C(T_1,...,T_k), and for any parameter value t in C^k for which the specialization f_t is defined and dominant, let delta(f_t) = lim_{n->infinity} deg(f_t^n)^(1/n), where deg(g) is the common degree of a homogeneous presentation of g after canceling common factors; similarly define delta(f) for the generic map f. Is it true that for every epsilon > 0, the exceptional set E_epsilon = { t in C^k : delta(f_t) <= delta(f) - epsilon } is not Zariski dense in C^k? In particular, when k = 1, must E_epsilon be finite?
justification: The draft is essentially a near-verbatim paraphrase of Conjecture 14.13, including the displayed exceptional set (14.2) and its one-parameter consequence. The immediately preceding Example 14.12 is the paper's motivating example for drops in dynamical degree inside families, and Definition 14.2 supplies the meaning of delta as dynamical degree. The draft's final sentence is not part of Conjecture 14.13 itself; it comes from the lead-in to Conjecture 14.14, which the paper presents only as a possible route to proving Conjecture 14.13. To make the question fully stand-alone and faithful, one must also spell out the generic-member meaning of the unsubscripted f in delta(f), the projective-space rational-map setup, and the degree/dynamical-degree definitions. Theorem 14.15 records that Conjectures 14.14 and 14.13 are known when N = 2.
